page_placements.theme: Parameter estimation and in-sample loss can decouple from prediction error

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper analytically derives a two-sided peak in coefficient variance for a purification-induced linear inverse problem, using a different setup and measure from test-error double descent. Its results bear narrowly on V6.
record.gate_note: The paper does not sweep deep-network size, training epochs, or sample size, and does not measure test error. Its double-descent analysis concerns coefficient variance under an assumed isotropic target-noise model. The paper also distinguishes that variance from state-action loss. Qualitative remarks that ridge regularization or eigenvalue cutoffs make the pole finite are not results from an applied regularization comparison.
record.test_reason: The paper maps a black-hole purification onto a linear inverse problem and invokes double descent only as an analogy. Its double-descent-related result is the textbook Marchenko-Pastur inverse-moment formula for unregularized coefficient variance, V(α)=σ²α/(1−α) or σ²/(α−1). That is a parameter-sensitivity measure, not test or prediction risk. The authors say explicitly that they do not identify it with out-of-sample prediction risk. The noisy state-action loss they do derive, σ² min(α,1), has no pole and is in-sample. No model size, epoch or sample-count sweep of test error is reported. No regularization is applied, and no label-noise comparison is made. This is a related but different construct, so it goes under fits_no_version rather than a V6 test.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors link the Page point to a rank and conditioning threshold. They limit the double-descent analogy to a two-sided peak in coefficient variance, explicitly not prediction risk, state-action loss or decoding error.
record.recipe_differences: The paper formulates a black-hole purification inverse problem and derives its coefficient variance using Marchenko-Pastur results; it does not reproduce the original deep-network or test-error experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The variance result assumes known D, isotropic target-noise covariance, no regularization, and an asymptotic fixed aspect ratio. The paper states that general noise covariance depends on its overlap with Gram eigendirections.

fits_no_version.finding: In a purification-induced linear inverse problem, the unregularized coefficient variance diverges as α=P/N approaches 1 from both sides (standard Marchenko-Pastur inverse moments).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Estimator coefficient variance in unregularized least squares or minimum-norm solutions peaks at the interpolation threshold.

fits_no_version.finding: The in-sample noise contribution to state-action loss is σ² min(α,1), with no interpolation pole.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In this inverse problem, coefficient sensitivity can diverge at interpolation while the in-sample loss contribution stays finite.

record.problems: The relevant result is an analytical inverse-problem calculation under an assumed isotropic target-noise model, not an empirical test of generalization error. The paper states that no measurement protocol for target amplitudes is specified and that D and target amplitudes are treated as known. It does not evaluate regularization experimentally or analytically in detail.
record.rows_left_out: No rows for the Page entropy, rank transition, or minimum reconstruction error: they do not measure a version's named test-error, complexity, or regularization outcome. No separate row for the paper's qualitative regularization remarks because no regularized comparison is reported.

record.verdict_notes: This is a theoretical physics analogy paper. The variance formula is a cited random-matrix result applied to a new interpretation. Ridge or cutoff regularization making the pole finite is stated but never computed. The reader's V6 'supports' label is removed because coefficient variance is not the test-error behaviour V6 names.

The paper derives coefficient variance under isotropic target perturbations, but does not test label noise, multiple or triple peaks, or optimally tuned regularization. It makes qualitative statements about ridge or cutoff regularization without evaluating those methods.

rows.subject: purification-induced linear inverse problem (D ∈ C^{N×P})
rows.operation_detail: Derives asymptotic coefficient variance using the Marchenko-Pastur inverse moments under isotropic additive target noise.
rows.measure: coefficient variance per black-hole component V(α)
rows.value: V(α) = σ² α/(1−α) for 0 < α < 1; V(α) = σ²/(α−1) for α > 1
rows.locator: Section III.C, Eq. (41); Appendix A, Eqs. (50)–(52)
rows.note: The derived variance rises toward the interpolation point from either side. This is coefficient sensitivity, not test or prediction risk.
rows.check: Coefficient variance under an assumed isotropic target-noise model is a sensitivity measure, not test or prediction risk. The authors explicitly disclaim identifying it with prediction risk. The value is the standard Marchenko-Pastur inverse-moment result (cited lecture notes, ref. 13), not a new measurement. It cannot show V6's test-error peak driven by noise or variance.

rows.operation_detail: Evaluates the unregularized inverse-Gram coefficient variance at the interpolation point.
rows.value: diverges; the ensemble average of the unregularized inverse Gram matrix also diverges at exact square dimension
rows.note: The paper notes that an individual finite square realization is invertible with probability one, while the ensemble average still diverges.
rows.check: Same construct as r1: the divergence of the unregularized inverse-Gram variance at α=1. This is not test error, so it does not bear on any version.
